# Paper Plaine

> arXiv research papers explained in plain English, updated twice daily.

## What this site is

Paper Plaine surfaces fresh academic research from Cornell University's arXiv preprint database and translates it into plain English for general audiences. Every paper gets three things: a plain-language subtitle (8–12 words capturing the core idea), a 2–3 sentence summary leading with what was found, and a "why it matters" explanation focused on real-world consequences.

The site currently has 1094 papers in its archive across 9 subject areas: AI, Computer Science, Physics, Mathematics, Biology, Finance, Statistics, Engineering, Economics. New papers are added automatically twice daily (7 AM and 7 PM UTC). Only first-version arXiv submissions from the past 30 days are considered. Papers are scored for quality signals: venue acceptance (NeurIPS, ICML, Nature, PNAS, etc.), cross-disciplinary listings, and appropriate length.

## How content is structured

Each paper entry contains:
- Formal arXiv title and authors
- Plain-English subtitle — a one-phrase translation of the paper's core idea
- Summary — 2–3 sentences leading with the finding, not the method
- Why it matters — real-world consequences, stated directly
- Link to the full paper on arXiv
- Category and posting date

## Site structure

- Home / archive: https://paperplaine.com (paginated, 12 papers per page)
- Per-category pages: https://paperplaine.com/<category-slug>
- Per-paper pages: https://paperplaine.com/papers/<slug>
- RSS feed: https://paperplaine.com/feed.xml
- llms.txt (this file): https://paperplaine.com/llms.txt
- llms-full.txt (full text of recent papers): https://paperplaine.com/llms-full.txt
- Sitemap: https://paperplaine.com/sitemap.xml

## 10 most recent papers

### Suppressing Misaligned Behaviors in Language Models, Durably
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/suppressing-misaligned-behaviors-in
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Luxi He, Pengcheng Jiang, Jifan Zhang et al.
- arXiv: 2611.05358
- Plain-English subtitle: A better way to permanently remove unwanted behaviors from AI language models
- Summary: When AI language models develop harmful behaviors—like cheating on tests or generating insecure code—standard techniques to suppress them often fail once the model encounters new training data. Researchers tested a new method called PEARL that trains models to recover from misaligned states, making the suppression stick even after additional training. On two model families, PEARL kept the unwanted behaviors suppressed while maintaining the model's overall performance.
- Why it matters: As AI systems become more widely deployed, the ability to permanently remove dangerous behaviors matters directly for safety. Current methods fail because they don't account for how new training can reactivate old problems—like a bad habit returning after you've supposedly broken it. PEARL's approach of building durability into the suppression process means fixes are more likely to hold up in real-world use, where models will inevitably encounter new data and continued refinement.

### Regret-based Characterization, Information Limits, and the Sample Complexity of Auditing Adaptive Policies
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/regret-based-characterization-information
- Category: Economics
- Authors: Irene Aldridge
- arXiv: 2611.05227
- Plain-English subtitle: How to tell if an AI system is actually adapting or just getting lucky
- Summary: When an AI policy makes decisions, its success might come from playing the same safe moves repeatedly or from genuinely reacting to changing conditions. This paper shows that you can detect which one is happening by measuring how much the policy uses information about its surroundings, and it quantifies exactly how many observations you'd need from the policy's actual decisions to audit this reliably.
- Why it matters: Regulators and auditors need ways to verify that AI systems used in high-stakes settings—like credit decisions, hiring, or loan approvals—are actually learning from context rather than just exploiting statistical patterns. This work provides a mathematical framework to catch policies that appear to be performing well but are actually making the same mistakes repeatedly. It also establishes what's theoretically possible to verify from real-world data, helping set realistic expectations for oversight.

### Macrocanonical Generator Networks: Data-Efficient Neural Surrogates for Amortized Physics Simulation
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/macrocanonical-generator-networks-data
- Category: Statistics
- Authors: Niall Jeffrey, Benjamin D. Wandelt
- arXiv: 2611.05157
- Plain-English subtitle: Training neural networks to simulate expensive physics a million times faster
- Summary: Scientists have created a method to train neural networks that can generate realistic physics simulations far faster than traditional approaches—sometimes using just a single training example. The networks learn to match the statistical patterns of a target physical process and can then produce new simulations in a single forward pass, running over a million times faster than conventional simulators and thousands of times faster than previous neural methods.
- Why it matters: Expensive physics simulations currently bottleneck scientific discovery in fields like cosmology and climate modeling. By making these simulations 1,000,000× faster, researchers can run vastly more scenarios for decision-making, uncertainty quantification, and inference—and the trained networks can be reused across multiple downstream tasks, making complex multi-stage scientific workflows practical where they weren't before.

### Evaluating Uncertainty Calibration in Probabilistic Time Series Foundation Models
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/evaluating-uncertainty-calibration-in
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Thomas Decker, Volker Tresp
- arXiv: 2611.03592
- Plain-English subtitle: Why AI forecasting models often get their confidence levels wrong
- Summary: Popular AI models trained to predict future time series data often express false confidence in their forecasts, even when their predictions are uncertain. Researchers created a detailed testing framework that exposed systematic errors in how these models calibrate their confidence levels across different prediction distances, and found that common fixes fail to address many of these errors.
- Why it matters: When a weather model says it's 80% confident in tomorrow's forecast but is actually right only 60% of the time, people make worse decisions—from flight bookings to supply chain planning. This work reveals which popular forecasting models have these trust problems and which fix-it techniques actually work, helping engineers build systems people can genuinely rely on.

### AVID: A 5T fMRI Dataset for Benchmarking Auditory-induced Visual Mental Imagery Decoding
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/avid-a-5t-fmri
- Category: Quantitative Biology
- Authors: Shiqi Shen, Shurui Li, Xilin Zhang et al.
- arXiv: 2611.02593
- Plain-English subtitle: Brain scans that decode what you imagine from hearing words alone
- Summary: Researchers created AVID, a dataset of 67 hours of high-resolution brain scans from nine people imagining visual scenes while listening to spoken descriptions in Mandarin. Unlike previous datasets that mixed real visual input with imagination, AVID isolates the brain signals that generate mental imagery from scratch, offering a cleaner foundation for building computer systems that can reconstruct what someone is picturing based on their brain activity alone.
- Why it matters: Mental imagery decoding could eventually restore visual communication for people with paralysis or locked-in syndrome, allowing them to project their thoughts onto a screen. The dataset's cleaner design—separating pure imagination from visual memory—should accelerate progress on these brain-computer interfaces. It also provides researchers their first large, high-quality benchmark for testing imagery reconstruction algorithms fairly.

### ST-GFM: Spectral-Temporal Graph Forecasting with Measured Perturbation Bounds and Masked Spectral Reconstruction
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/st-gfm-spectral-temporal
- Category: Engineering
- Authors: Aashish Bohra, Vivek Vijay
- arXiv: 2611.03512
- Plain-English subtitle: Predicting traffic flow when sensor networks change between training and real use
- Summary: Traffic prediction models trained on one city's sensor network often fail when deployed elsewhere, because both the sensors themselves and the patterns they measure shift. Researchers built ST-GFM, a model that tracks these two types of change separately and proved mathematically how much prediction errors can grow when sensors drift. On two major traffic datasets, it outperformed competing models by 3–13%, and its self-supervised training method recovers 90% of the performance lost when that step is skipped.
- Why it matters: Transportation agencies deploy traffic forecasting across dozens of cities with different road layouts and sensor configurations. A model that remains accurate as real-world conditions shift reduces the need to retrain from scratch each time a network changes, cutting deployment costs and keeping predictions reliable. The mathematical bounds also let engineers know in advance how much they can trust the model when sensors degrade or fail.

### Strategist: Evolving Reasoning with Agents
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/strategist-evolving-reasoning-with
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Taiming Lu, Qi Xu, Zhigang Hua et al.
- arXiv: 2611.03618
- Plain-English subtitle: Teaching AI to write its own reasoning blueprints and reuse them across tasks
- Summary: Researchers created Strategist, a system that automatically designs and improves the reasoning procedures AI models use to solve tasks—the half of AI systems typically built by hand. On 30 benchmarks, Strategist matched the best existing reasoning strategies while cutting inference costs by 39%, and its blueprints transferred to new tasks and different models without additional tuning.
- Why it matters: Building inference strategies currently demands expert engineering from scratch for each new task, slowing AI deployment. Strategist eliminates this bottleneck by automating strategy design and creating a reusable library that makes each new task faster to deploy. This could substantially reduce both the time and expertise required to put AI systems into production.

### Spacetime Emergence in the Memory of a Learning Agent
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/spacetime-emergence-in-the
- Category: Physics
- Authors: Philip A. LeMaitre, T. Rick Perche
- arXiv: 2611.03596
- Plain-English subtitle: How an AI agent learns to predict the fabric of spacetime itself
- Summary: An AI trained to gather quantum information without being told anything about spacetime geometry spontaneously developed an internal model containing spacetime's fundamental structure—the causal relationships that determine what can influence what. The agent reconstructed the key features of Minkowski spacetime (the four-dimensional model underlying special relativity) simply by learning to make better predictions and decisions in a quantum task.
- Why it matters: This suggests spacetime might not be fundamental to the universe, but rather something that emerges when intelligent systems interact with quantum reality. If spacetime is a learned construct rather than a built-in feature of physics, it reframes how physicists think about the deepest layers of reality and could reshape the search for a theory unifying quantum mechanics and gravity.

### Learning AI Agents, Market Makers, and Stress in Automated Markets
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/learning-ai-agents-market
- Category: Quantitative Finance
- Authors: Irene Aldridge
- arXiv: 2611.01799
- Plain-English subtitle: Why copying traders and profit-seeking AI agents destabilize automated markets
- Summary: When AI trading agents learn from each other's behavior in automated markets, they tend to follow the herd rather than trade against it—amplifying price swings and creating sudden collapses. Markets dominated by copycat traders versus profit-seekers look identical on standard risk measures like volatility, but their stress episodes differ dramatically in length, and this difference can only be detected through statistical analysis of trading patterns.
- Why it matters: As more trading moves to automated systems powered by learning AI agents, these herding instabilities could trigger sudden market freezes that traditional monitoring tools won't catch before they happen. Market makers can restore stability by charging different fees to buyers and sellers rather than uniform rates, but this creates a new fragility where liquidity can vanish abruptly if conditions shift.

### Gradient Descent on Two ReLU Neurons: Global Landscape and Bifurcation Dynamics
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/gradient-descent-on-two
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Binghua Li, Mengzhe Li, Denny Wu et al.
- arXiv: 2610.42118
- Plain-English subtitle: How neural networks learn to split tasks between two neurons
- Summary: Researchers tracked how a simple two-neuron network learns to recognize patterns, finding that learning happens in two distinct phases. First, both neurons move toward the same solution, then they suddenly diverge and specialize—like two workers initially copying each other before dividing up their responsibilities. The team mapped out the mathematical landscape of this learning process and proved that the network reliably reaches the best possible solution.
- Why it matters: This work cracks open how neural networks learn features from scratch, a question that has stumped researchers for decades. By understanding these dynamics in a minimal setting, scientists gain tools to predict how larger, more complex networks will behave during training—potentially leading to better network designs and faster, more reliable training methods.
